And you can see, it allows you to zoom all the way in with no loss of resolution whatsoever. Basically, it's called resolution-independent graphics. So, pretty much all of the corporate logos that you see and typesetting and everything else like that is done with vector-based graphics, as opposed to bitmap graphics, which are integrated pixels. My project is clipping suburbia, Japan, and one of the things that I'm really interested in is how algorithms see the world, and how we're affected by the algorithmic soup that we swim these days. So, I have a bit written here. Moments jam up against each other. Staring from a train hurtling through the city, the world flashes by. A mangled jumble of screen impressions seen and not seen, racing forward in a distraction of thoughts, thrown out by cloud-computed algorithms. We're making a new digital world for ourselves. Gone is our leisurely pace of thought and lifestyle. And driven by frictionless connectivity, this digital life is a headlong rush.

These photos are an expression of the speed, the cascade of experiences that are the defining aspect of this brave new world. And while my work is, on the one hand, an exploration of how this digital world feels to me, I'm also interested in the question of how the algorithmic devices we populate our lives with experience this very same environment. In other words, how would an AI see the world? The Clipping Suburbia series is generative at its core. The content of the images are compiled entirely by the algorithmic processes of my iPhone's AI as it struggles to cope with the novel experience of recording a panorama from a train window speeding through the landscape at 40 to 50 miles per hour.

But, in this struggle, it creates these wonderful images of time and space compressed, of fragments flowing together to form digitized impressions of the world racing by. But, in the end, these results still pose a question. And that is, will AIs see in the same beautifully formed, 3D technicolor renderings as we do, or… Could their world maybe actually be more like this, a constellation of fragmentary images? Or even, perhaps they see something unseeable to us, something entirely of their own imagining. The two worlds, digital space and our experiences of tangible world, are not separate. As we continue incorporating artificial intelligence into our daily lives, we merge. We increasingly experience our world through their eyes, through their senses. And that, I feel, is one of the most important points of this work. For me, especially these smaller images, really feel like the world these days. It feels like everything is rushing too fast. Before you get one thought, another thought comes Intruding upon it. You can never really finish putting together ideas before there's something else happening, and you have to jump away to something else, so… On Expressionists, this is expressionism, after all, on an expressionist point of view, that's a lot of what I feel is expressed in this, the speed and the fragmentary nature of the world we live in today. She's an artist on our Techspressionist Artists Index, and a graphic designer. With this exhibition titled Creative Graphics, she created a space where fine art and graphic design could meet.

Since the venue was the Museum of Calligraphy. Which is found inside the Seoul Arts Center, I decided to make works that contain glyphs, or Roman alphabet letter forms. I showed 30 paintings in this Lumen Suite, and they were displayed via a slideshow on a TV monitor, wall-mounted in portrait orientation. And when I mention the glyphs or the characters, you can see the Y's… Here… and… you can see my pointer. Okay, and then zeros, there's an elongated zero here, and a couple of zeros there.

Here is… An ampersand, which is one of my favorite characters. And it's made out of wireframe in this work, which makes reference to the underlying mathematical order of the form. It also references the constructivist and Bauhaus movements. Bauhaus is kind of a favorite of mine. But the severity of this wireframe is lightened by the color palette, which is very fanciful and non-technical. And for me, it recalls the color palette of Rococo art, paintings in particular. The… Custom brushes I make resemble wire in this Work, so you can see there, and there, and also… The colors of these brushes are derived from color in the painting, so if you see this red up here… The brush took on the same hue of red there, mixed with pink.

And also there. And these… I made you a close-up, so… these… Brushes are… Standing out because of the combination of shadow and light that is on them. And also the high-res files, because all of these paintings are done on a canvas that is 6,000 by 8,000 pixels.

And here's another example from another painting of the wire brush, and behind it, you can see very atmospheric and very diffuse brushes. And this one down here, because it's blown up, it doesn't really gleam, but when it's smaller, it looks quite golden. I'm always trying to get metallic… Things going on in my paintings. So this painting here is full of cheroscuro, or an interplay between shadow and light. And I really… I was recently in Amsterdam, and I was able to look at some paintings by Rembrandt in the Rijksmuseum, and this drama that Karascuro makes is always really, something I love, and here's… you can see in this shape.

Just how strong the play between light and dark is. The show in Seoul led to an invitation from a curator, Hong Gyeon Mok, from GMAP. And GMAP is in Gwangju, South Korea. Hello everyone, my name is Colin Goldberg, and I'm a Techspressionist. Welcome to Techspressionist Salon Number 102. Today is Thursday, January 8th. 2026, and this salon's title is Art Science Interaction. Our salons are a time and place in cyberspace where artists gather once a month to hang out, share their work, and discuss matters relating to art, philosophy, and technology. These meetups were conceived as a modern counterpart to the surrealist salons of the 1920s, in which artists could meet informally to socialize and discuss ideas.

Techspressionism is a 100% volunteer-based international artist community. So That's my little blurb about… Techspressionism and, our salon, so, all of you are more than welcome, or people viewing on YouTube are more than welcome to join us. You can find out, what the upcoming salon is at Techspressionism.Com slash salon. And also get the Zoom links there. There's also an archive of the last 101 salons on that page. So, our moderator today is Heidi Boir, who is an interdisciplinary artist, experienced designer, creative technologist, and academic researcher who interrogates the neurobiological and sociocultural effects of media and technology.

She studies the role of the body, the senses, and emotion in human perception and social change. Boivaire is mapping the world's first media genome, while taking great care with its far-reaching ethical implications. A specialist in modern American art, Harrison has served as the curator of the Parish Art Museum and Guildhall Museum and was guest curator at the Queens Museum. Christiane Paul is professor of the Center for the Arts at the University of New York. I'm also a member of the Pollock Foundation and New York State Council on the Arts, and currently I live and work in the Green Mountains of Southern Vermont with my wife Donna and our daughter Aya. I first used the term Techspressionism in 2011 as the title for a solo exhibition in Southampton, New York.

Techspressionism, which is the topic of our discussion today, is defined in Wiktionary as an artistic approach in which technology is utilized as a means to express emotional experience. Some of the philosophical framework around Techspressionism is the idea that the individual is the subject of the exhibition. The text is outlined in the Techspressionist Manifesto, which I first published on Medium in 2014. This text was inspired by artistic manifestos of the past, including Marinetti's Futurist Manifesto and Breton's Surrealist Manifesto.

Techspressionism was first described as a movement in the Wired article if Picasso had a MacBook Pro in 2014 and received its first television coverage in a 2015 episode of the PBS show Art Loft. The use of Techspressionism as a hashtag on social media has long been a trend. The term has allowed technology-based artists to self-identify with the term. Since the summer of 2020, there have been over 49,000 posts published on Instagram using the hashtag Techspressionism.

The use of the hashtag has functioned as a primary research mechanism in the curatorial process of developing an artist index, an online community for artists using technology in their work. Over the past two years, Techspressionism has developed into an online community, including artists from over 40 countries. The project's development was inspired in part by the concept of social sculpture invented by the artist Joseph Beuys.

Techspressionist artists meet in regularly scheduled online salons to share work and discuss ideas. These recorded meetups are conceived of as a modern counterpart to the surrealist salons of the past. Ann Spalter, artist and author of Computer and the Visual Arts, published by Addison Wesley, has described Techspressionism as follows.

Techspressionism is introduced in the world of art. It is used as a new art historical term to describe fine artists using digital technology to convey subjective emotional content. Techspressionism distinguishes expressive fine art from such genres as digital art, which can include animated movies and video games, as well as from new media works that may not embody convincing artistic intent. The subjective lens of the individual artist, rather than the product of a corporate studio, is what connects Techspressionism to its predecessor, expressionism.

Techspressionists present the world from a subjective perspective, distorting it radically in order to evoke moods or ideas, seeking to express their emotional experience rather than physical reality. And I'm really pleased today that those 5 original members who got together five years ago are here today to share their recollections. And before we get them talking about that very first meeting.

I want to read and share just a little biographical information about each of them. Colin Goldberg coined the term Techspressionism in 2011 to describe his hybrid practice combining painting, digital media, and technology. In September 2020, he initiated the first Techspressionism meetup. Which set the goal of building an artist community around the term, one that now spans over 45 countries. A Pollack Krasner grant recipient. Goldberg's work has been featured in the New York Times, Wired, NPR, and PBS, and his Metagraphs series of augmented reality works will be presented in a solo exhibition at the Cape Cod Museum of Art in the summer of 2027.

Helen A. Harrison is an art historian, journalist, author, and retired director of the Pollack Krasner House and Study Center in East Hampton, New York. She is currently president of Arts Center at Duck Creek, also in East Hampton. She has been an advisor to the Expressionism Project since 2020. Patrick Lichty is a multifaceted media artist, writer, curator, designer, and educator whose career spans more than three decades. His work engages with augmented and virtual reality, generative and telecommunications art, and machine drawing, critically examining how media and technology shape human perception.

A CalArts Herb Alpert Fellow and Whitney Biennial Exhibitor, Litke has established himself as a significant voice in exploring the cultural impact of emerging technologies. Steve Miller has worked at the intersection of art, science, and technology since 1980. His projects include collaborations with Nobel laureate Rod McKinnon on human protein research, work at Brookhaven National Lab, and lectures at CERN in Geneva. For over a decade, he developed Health of the Planet, a photographic project examining Brazil's Amazon through X-rays of its flora and fauna.

Published in three monographs by G Editions. Miller's work has been exhibited internationally in cities including Paris, Rio, Hong Kong, London, and New York, and most recently at the Academy of Sciences in Washington, D.C. He also designs custom surfboards, skate decks, and fashion, teaches at the School of Visual Arts, and is co-founder of art software platform Arternal. Oz Van Rosen. And I said, they're all really pretty fertile places to… Fertile places to go. And, you know, in the beginning, I, you know, I… I think, like Steve, I wasn't… you know, I said, okay, this is… this is kind of a brand. I said, this is, you know, movement community, whatever, let's see what happens. But I think what's interesting is that over the 5 years, you know, there was, you know, that show at the Southampton, and, you know, things were still growing, calling said, you know, is this… you know, is this turning into… is this turning into something? And I said, you know, or, you know, is this gonna keep going? And I said, I, you know, I think it's… I think so. And, you know, 3 years later.

Yeah, it just seems very, very solid. So, you know, I think… you know, movements are often based around, you know, kind of, you know, kind of, you know, central notions, but I think that, in many ways, to expressionism, and I think this idea that, you know, I popped through my head, I think also Helen's, of this being kind of like a fourth iteration of, of, of, you know, expressionist thought. You know, it's, I think it also reflects the culture in that of… of being… of distributed culture of networks. In other words, like, the… you know, there isn't really a set Ideology, but the thing is, there's an impulse, and I think that there's, a people wanting to be together and wanting to have these… share these emotional experiences and that sort of thing through technology, which, you know, is kind of endemic to art, but on the other hand, it's… I think that there's something… Shared and, you know, and I think that's what keeps, you know, Techspressionism running, and, you know, whatever that is, it seems to have it, so that's great.

So, that's my… that's my spiel.

segments.speaker: Michael Pierre Price
segments.text: Thanks, Patrick. Okay, Helen, what are your thoughts?

segments.speaker: Helen A. Harrison
segments.text:
Well, Patrick raises a very important point, which is that it… The technology aspect of it is actually a double whammy. You have the technology as a way of creating, as a way of enabling artists to create things that they couldn't create otherwise, but also the distribution element, where you can get your word out to so much broader audience, not only the people who are working in the genre, in the movement. Or using that as their impulse. But also reaching people who would never know about it otherwise, through the internet.

And through the electronic media that are so prevalent today. So, it's building on two different aspects of technology that… both of which contribute to the richness of the movement itself. I think Colin invited me on because, well, I had known him for years through his father, who was a teacher at Southampton College, where my husband also was teaching, so through his… through the faculty, that's how we met. But when he approached me in 2011 and asked me if I would write a little intro to the catalog for the show that he mentioned, he was talking then about How technology, or how… how a movement, or how an impulse like Techspressionism Where did it fit?

You know, if you're thinking of something in terms of, like, for example, surrealism, which was a defined movement, it had a guy who was in charge, Andre Breton, it had a manifesto, it had membership. In fact, Breton said who was in and who was out. I said, let's not do that. We don't want to have the Pope of Techspressionism, like, Breton was the Pope of Surrealism, because that's A too hierarchical, and B, who cares what this guy thinks? You know, this is really reaching out to a much broader and much more diverse group of practitioners.

So, what he really wanted me to do, I think, was to relate the impulse to other impulses that had kind of a similar, origin story. And being the head of the Paula Krasner House, and knowing a few things about abstract expressionism, that was a way of making the connection, because the whole point, to me Is that it's expressionistic. That the technology is the means to an end. And this was Pollack's famous statement, it doesn't matter how the paint is put on, as long as something is being said. Technique is just a means of arriving at a statement.

And there are, you know, other examples of people thinking about this concept and elucidating it in terms of contemporary art. One of them I quoted in the catalog. This is the catalog. You see that, my bookmark. This is the catalog for the Expressionism exhibition from Southampton Cultural Center… sorry, Southampton Arts Center. And I quoted Paul Valerie, who said, we must expect great innovations to transform the entire technique of the arts, thereby affecting artistic intervention… invention itself, and perhaps even bringing about an amazing change in our very notion of art.

That was written in 1928. Now, by that time, I think the photography debate had been pretty much settled. But, you know, there were other technologies 20th century technologies that were revolutionizing thought. And they were not universally accepted, they were controversial. But at the same time, they helped to move Creative endeavor forward by bringing new potential, new possibilities. And certainly the abstract expressionists, who didn't like the term, in fact, but it was actually invented in Germany.

In post-war Germany in 1919 was when it was coined. By, an artist called Oswald Herzog. And the… Idea was that it was supposed to be something in the way that surrealism is more about dreams. It was supposed to be more about spirit. Which I think is why Kandinsky was one of their avatars, that Kandinsky represented this so strongly, that it was an art that was above reality, beyond reality, but in the spiritual realm, rather than in the dream world.

And he articulated this quite clearly, and it was never really picked up on until Alfred Barr used it in 1929 in conjunction with Kandinsky, talking about Kandinsky. And then in 1946, an American critic used it, thinking that he was coining it, sort of like going back to Cohen and Oz, you know, bringing up these things at the same time. And yet they flow from one another. So there was a kind of continuity there, because ironically, the critic was talking about Hans Hoffman.

Who used the term back in 1915. So, you know, it was like… it came full circle. But the technology side is… that's the means, and then the expressionism is the end. So this was a nice, I thought, a very congenial marriage of terms. I don't care what your husband or wife thought about it at the time. I think it works great.

segments.speaker: Michael Pierre Price
segments.text:
Thank you, Helen. That's a great perspective. This is so fascinating to me, because… The five of you got together. None of you could really say where you really thought this was going to go, and obviously we now have a 5-year history. That initial get-together, where we are today, and so much, in my opinion, has transpired in that timeframe. Have you been surprised, and anybody can chime in here, have you been surprised at how things have Evolved without necessarily As you mentioned, Helen, without having an Andre Breton saying, this is where we're going and this is how we're heading. My opinion has been that the decentralized nature, although Colin has been, obviously, a very central figure in this, he has been reluctant to be the Andre Breton of the community.

And he is basically… Asked everybody who's interested, if you have a cool idea, run with it. How did we get here, and what surprises, and how do you… how do you… how do you read the history right now of this 5-year period that we've gone through? Because there's so much that's happened.

segments.speaker: Steve Miller
segments.text: What's the problem?

segments.speaker: Helen A. Harrison
segments.text:
For me, it was the, the exhibition. When we started talking about doing a physical show, because up till that point, it had just been online. And the community was building, and people were sharing ideas. But then you say, well, who's going to see this? Only the people who are online. But if it's a real art movement, a real, an international impulse, it would be great to be able to manifest this in physical terms, so that you can see the variety all in one place.

Instead of having to go online and going into the different forums. And once the exhibition idea started to gel. I was just absolutely stupefied by the number of people, the number of different approaches, the number of… I mean, you know, think about people All over the world doing this without realizing that there was a community, and then suddenly becoming part of that community. And it just… it just seemed to me you know, being a museum person myself, and I like to look at art on walls or on a pedestal, I like the physical stuff.

And even when it's electronic, if it's on a monitor or something like that, just to be able to sit in front of it and contemplate it, rather than having to go on Zoom, off Zoom, whatever. And I felt that the show and, you know, and it has had a couple of afterlives, that that really helped to make the movement solidify.

segments.speaker: Oz Van Rosen
segments.text:
I would agree with that. I remember thinking, wow, it's real, you know? And yeah, it was so amazing to see all the different artists, and I agree with you, I like seeing… we're just so inundated with digital images now, and our eyes are always on some screen, big or small. And it almost… I hate to use the word cheapens it, but, you know, just the sheer volume of images that… that flow through us, you know, we just see them for, like, a few seconds, that to see them in their physical forms.

Especially the installations. It was so… such a wonderful feeling to see that.

segments.speaker: Patrick Lichty
segments.text:
One thing I think is interesting is I think that one thing we forget, even digital art is material culture, you know? So, I mean, on one hand is that, I mean, there's… you know, even computers, hard drives, etc, screens, and so on, but I think, really, I think the suppleness of the, you know, of what this is. You know, it's engaged, you know, material, you know, physical art, digital art, VR… you know, and so on. And actually, Nagin and I, before, the, you know, the Southampton show, we had put a, put together about, maybe about a third of the exhibition at the International Digital Media and Arts Association, conference.

In Winona, with about 20, 30 artists, Yeah, that… out of a whole set of 90 here at Winona State University, so I think that's a little, you know, a little… Preamble to, you know, things like that, and I think having those artists, you know, like Colin and Tommy and Cynthia and that sort of thing, you know, in that space. You know, was, you know, a really, was a, you know, I mean, just a really good proof of concept. Yeah, but I think on one hand, you know, you've got, you know, you've got this, this set of practices that, you know, this particular set, you know, this, this entire kind of, I'd say, philosophy.

You know, runs itself to. You know, and then on the other hand, it's the fact that it's, you know, while Colin and I have conversations about terms like social sculpture, you know, the one thing is, is that, I think, you know, the social component, you know, is extremely strong. In other words, in different models, you've got the co-worker, you've got the… you know, you've got the salons, you've got, you know, you know, people meeting up, you have, you know, so… you know, I think there are different… Opinions, you know, to… you know, that make this, you know, such a… such a solid endeavor, and, and I think this is, you know, the one thing there have been thoughts about having, you know, having a, What, a journal or an almanac, which, you know, kind of get tossed around once in a while.

You know, I think there's just enough people with enough, enthusiasm, you know, that… you know, that, you know, enough gets thrown on the wall, you know, something, you know, something sticks. And maybe at another one point or another, there might be a journal, but, you know, the, you know. You know, the… just so many, you know, so many salons, the exhibitions are going strong, you know, it's like we're doing the project in, Uzbekistan, and, you know, and then going out… people are going out to LA.

Yeah, I just think it's really, you know, this idea of this, of this… you know, Hydra in terms of practice, and also from… of social engagement, you know, that has its face forward out into the public. And this is, you know, why, you know, people know it so well, and, you know, that it's had such traction.

segments.speaker: Steve Miller
segments.text:
Michael, just to answer the first part of your question, the David Byrne question, how did we get here? Letting the days go by. And, you know, really, how we got here is that we did have an organizer, and someone, you know, that Helen mentioned, you know, part of this Is there was a means of distribution, and, you know, Colin set up a structure, right? He created the website, he got us all to meet the first meeting, right, 5 years ago. And then, building out, you know, it doesn't… you know, the community can't exist unless there's a place for them all to meet. Patrick mentioned ThingNet, which I was a part of, you know, you create these sort of communities and a structure, and with the website, the meetups, there was, you know, several years' worth of energy that brought in… and then, you know, Colin's determination to make it international, and make it very open, and to use the hashtag, which was, you know, one of the key ways that he used the internet to sort of, disseminate the meme.

So I think that how we got here, how did we get here, really has to do with the ability of Colin to match concept with the structure of the internet. So that got us All here to this place. And now, as everyone else has said, you know, there's… it's… anyone can plug into the structure, create a group within the group, set up an exhibition. I mean, it's really awesome. There was also an exhibition in New York City this year. There's one in Brooklyn, earlier.

I think it's Uzbekistan, and, there's gonna be Colin's solo show. So… Clearly. There is currently momentum, and I… and that momentum will continue, because there's going to be an exhibition in 2027. I guess the next thing is, is, you know. How… how will this… can it grow more? Will it survive? Is there new energy that's gonna come in? Will there be other forms of validation that have to happen, you know, within the curatorial community? And, and as… Technology becomes, you know, obviously AI as technology becomes the prevalent language of culture, and forget about art. I mean, it's intersected every aspect of our lives already, and it'll be really interesting to see if we are going to be… Emotionally.

Vulnerable and accessible in this sort of non-human structure. To keep it alive with our part of the conversation. So there's the technology that arrives, and then it's how we use that technology. And, you know, in my opinion, to humanize it, make it accessible, to translate it, to, perhaps even make it beautiful.

segments.speaker: Helen A. Harrison
segments.text:
Oh, I think it's beautiful already, but the beauty is created by the people who use it. It's not inherent in the system. The system is limited by human imagination, but the human imagination is not limited at all. So, I mean, first of all, hats off to Colin for taking on this whole project, but I remember when we first talked about the exhibition, I said. Be careful what you wish for. Because it's a lot of work! And just, I mean, what a herd of cats, you know, they're all over the world, and corralling that, all that energy, and getting it into a physical space was a big endeavor, and, you know, on that level.

As well as just the holding together the group online is really a major production, and I have to say, I think he pulled it off brilliantly.

segments.speaker: Colin Goldberg
segments.text: Well, thanks, Helen.

segments.speaker: Steve Miller
segments.text: Quick thing about the exhibition, you know, Colin did that, you know, a drone within the exhibition that flew through, and I think that's just such a marvelous way for anyone who's not able to see the exhibition to get another kind of As much as you could have a tactile experience, to really get a feeling of what it was like.

segments.speaker: Patrick Lichty
segments.text: Hmm?

segments.speaker: Colin Goldberg
segments.text:
Yeah, so the drone, was actually… it was piloted by a high school classmate of mine named Joanna Steidle. Who went to Southampton High School with me. We graduated in the same year. She actually lived on the same road as I grew up on, which was a dirt road at the time. And you know, I just thought this would be a really cool way to document the show. You know, I feel like as far as the surprises go, it was… it's just been an ongoing sequence of surprises. I think an early one was… when, Davonte Bradley, Davo, who… he moderated a lot of the early salons.

And he was one of the first people that I kind of actually called up, because I tagged his work with hashtag to expressionism, and then he reminded me, and then there were 3 fire emojis after it. And he's like. Like, I like that term, you know, and and then once he started getting involved with the group and the salons and everything like that, he said, you know, I feel like I've found my tribe. And I thought, like, wow, like, that's… that's pretty powerful, like, that's a reason to keep doing this, for people to feel like this is their place to be, and they're like-minded people. I mean, as far as, like, the ideology behind it, you know, the manifesto, like, the first version of the manifesto really was about that I feel like this is legitimate. That, you know, there's a number of points in it. I was just looking back on it, but that the first point, and I think the first three points are the important ones for me, the most important ones.

Are that the computer and technology in general is… are not separate from humankind, but a natural extension of us. The second one would be that technology is a continuum, which is as old as humanity, not a novelty or fad. And then the third one is that the computer is one of a long string of tools which have enabled human expression, including the typewriter, the camera, the printing press. The pen, the pencil, and paint. So, going all the way back, you know, when these things were invented, they were the high technology of the time. So I feel like, when people talk about technology nowadays.

It's just assumed that that's about computers and digital technology, whereas looking back. You know, I always think about Cindy Sherman as somebody who, you know, broke ground in defining herself as an artist who uses a camera to make her Her statements, her pictures, not a photographer. And I think that opened it up, and, you know, that opened up a lot of work that is photographic in nature to, To mainstream galleries, not segregated photography galleries.

You know, other… I mean, just the fact that Southampton Arts Center Bit on this idea and agreed to it was a big, huge surprise. Actually, it was Helen that suggested a show to begin with, because I was like, well, what do you think about this idea? She said, well, maybe put an exhibition together and see who sticks around. You know, and here we are, although Patrick seems to have lost his connection. But, you know, see who sticks around. And I think that, you know, it's gone way beyond what I ever could have anticipated. And, I remember at the time, Amy Kirwan was the director of Southampton Arts Center, and I pitched the idea to her, and I was like, well, the show could just be called Techspressionism, and she said, you know, it needs something else.

How about Techspressionism beyond, you know, beyond the digital? And I thought, well… Some of it is inherently digital, you know? Like, some of it is screen-based work, or animation, NFTs. To me, like, that constitutes What I would consider digital art. And you know, so we ended up just, you know, agreeing on this Techspressionism, digital and beyond, so it's digital as a jumping-off point, but then, you know. Sort of extrapolating into all these other areas, like painting, and printmaking, sculpture, and so on and so forth. Well, the common denominator, the common denominator is the expressionism part of it.

segments.speaker: Helen A. Harrison
segments.text: Technology is varied, and widely varied. You had printmaking, you had sculpture, you had all kinds of other things, but the idea is to have a subjective element that you are expressing something, it's not just graphic design, it's not just imagery, it's not branding or pop culture or whatever. It has to come from inside the artist, and then you find the technological way to express it, to get it out.

segments.speaker: Colin Goldberg
segments.text:
Yeah, no, that's a very good point, and I think at the first salon… well, there were two… two things that happened in the first salon that stick out of my mind, because the original definition when I first came up with this term was. An artistic style in which technology is utilized as a means to express emotional experience Rather than impressions of outside reality. And that was me pretty much just taking the, you know, very long-winded, definition, taking the Oxford definition of expressionism and of technology and, like, sticking them together. And I remember Oz said, you know, why don't you just get rid of, like, that whole end part about Rather than impressions of the outside world, especially because she was starting as… with photographic imagery, I assume that might have been part of the rationale behind it, so some of it was actually based in impressions of the outside world. It was just… Taking these things and working with them in a way that's, you know, expressive, personally expressive. And then Helen said, you know, why don't we just get rid of this word style altogether and replace it with the word approach?

And, you know, at that time, I couldn't really wrap my head around How important that has been, in terms of the group… Being so, or just, you know, the term being so applicable to so many different types of artists. Whether they're abstract or figurative artists, whatever the way they're using technology is. And this idea that it's expressionism, the expressionist aspect of it, you know, is what differentiates itself from Digital art, to me, which, you know, is applicable to things like video game design, or, mainstream media like Pixar movies. And when you, you know, look at digital art programs in college.

This is sort of, like, that's the end game, is that students graduate with a degree in digital art, and they go out into industry. So, this is, you know, for me, Techspressionism. The term is a differentiator, that it's individual artists using it to express themselves. You know, and with that, you know, and then just… yeah, I made a point out of it being, you know, self… based on self-identification, that is, like, you're a Techspressionist when you say you are. So the idea that if you like the term, then You're free to use it, no one has to approve you being part of the group or not part of the group, or whatever, you know? Like, and this idea of it being brought into common usage was a personal goal of mine in terms of Getting people together and seeing who, you know, who likes this as a term. So, a lot of people over the years, over the last 5 years, have said, you know.

Are you gonna trademark this? Are you gonna make it into a not-for-profit organization? Are you gonna make merch and sell t-shirts? And it's just like, no. You know, and this flies in the face of all marketing, but marketing generally The goal isn't to make something open source or, you know, universally applicable, and to bring something into common usage. It's to make it proprietary. You know, so the whole process has been really sort of like. You know, a little bit of an unraveling of, like, that part of my brain, but… and then seeing the way people take it and run with it. I mean, that's, to me, the most gratifying part of this, is seeing people like Tommy Mintz just say, hey, you know, like.

I'm teaching at this college in Brooklyn, and I have access to, you know, the Kingsborough Art Museum space. What do you think about putting a show together? And I was like, yeah. Go for it, you know? And I think the biggest surprise, actually, for me, is the way that the hashtag has propagated itself on its own. I mean… I have always been a fan of Richard Dawkins, who invented the term meme way before funny internet cat memes were a thing. It was to describe a field of study called memetics, which is based on genetics, and it's the idea of how, cultural content propagates.

Through hosts, which is a little spooky, but we are the hosts, and the memes propagate themselves through us. And this is something that, you know, through pop culture, meme turned into something else, the mainstream Definition of it, but I thought, you know, there's definitely validity to the theory, and that the internet is a really, you know, it's the most potent way that information is disseminated. And the hashtag really has… is the way that it's reached the most people, and it's… it's been adopted.

On its own. You know, it's the closest thing to anything viral that I've been a part of, because honestly, like, in the beginning, I was tagging people with a hashtag that I thought their work exemplified what I felt was Techspressionism. And I found a whole bunch of different artists that way, and consciously tried to find artists in different countries and different states, tagging them with this work, and then I'd send them a message, like. Hey, if you want, use the hashtag, and by the way, come to our salons. You know, and then it just started… it started spreading on its own, and now we're up to something like 82,000 posts on Instagram using the hashtag, and Renata Anishevska is the Instagram curator, and she's done an amazing job of Picking, you know, picking artists, working with them, highlighting them, and so forth, so it's been a big community effort. So, anyway, that's my…

segments.speaker: Helen A. Harrison
segments.text: Kind of…

segments.speaker: Colin Goldberg
segments.text: Input on that. What's been surprising is, like, everything, so…

segments.speaker: Michael Pierre Price
segments.text:
Well, as… well, as somebody who wasn't in the first meeting, although I did make it to the third salon, I have to say that there are two… two things that I've found have been so significant. One is that sense of finding your tribe. I cannot say… To… I just… it's really, you know, I found my peeps, and it's just the sense that… There's such a deep history with so many of the people here in this community who have used technology to create art for decades, and there's a wealth of history there. They've seen the technology change in advance.

And there's a real sense of community, of generosity, of support. And… and the other thing for me, the term Techspressionism. Has been a way in to talk about what I do, because it is so confounding for people who don't understand how art can be created using technology. That there's very little common lexicon that you can use for people to get it. And having a word that's sort of out there, that they're not quite sure, it's… it starts a conversation, and I really love that about… about that. And so I think those have been, for me.

Really, really, wonderful parts of being part of this community, this movement, this social sculpture, whatever. I think we should wrap up, so I'd like to leave each one of you with, you know, a couple minutes to share any… Ending thoughts that you might have about maybe where we're headed, or what you're hoping for, or just any, any thoughts about, what we've talked about today.

segments.text:

When he officially decided he was no longer going to be painting anymore, and he was only going to be using digital techniques.

Technically, in my mind, I think he's the first expressionist.

segments.speaker: Helen A. Harrison
segments.text: Well, I can't say I agree with you, because I think Warhol… if you take him at his word, which, of course, many people did not, because they didn't take him very seriously, he said he just wanted to be famous. And so whatever… it wasn't about expression. Remember, this is Techspressionism, where expression is paramount. It is actually about making images that sell well. And, of course, he really… most of his work, the work that was at the Whitney, the really important work was down in the gallery by the entrance, sort of off to the side where most people missed it, was his portraits.

segments.speaker: Oz Van Rosen
segments.text: He made a fortune!

segments.speaker: Helen A. Harrison
segments.text:
Doing portraits of celebrities. That was his bread and butter. The rest of the stuff was icing on the cake, because it didn't really sell that well. Even Castelli couldn't move it. He never got a good review in his entire career. And people considered him just, you know, jumped-up fashion illustrator. But it was… it was his brilliance at… at marketing and promotion. But I think that, really. For those of you who are new to the term Techspressionism, Techspressionism is an artistic approach in which technology is utilized as a means to express emotional experience. And we're a globalworked community of artists working with technology. As a community, we hold monthly virtual salons with fascinating presentations by various artist technologists. And also a group of us meet weekly on Zoom for a co-working session. And we organize art exhibitions and post artist interviews on the website.
